messages.subject: Sequenza 3.0.0 is out
messages.body_plain:
New sequenza release is on CRAN now.

Changes since 2.1.2:

 - Code cleanup and refactoring
 - Bug fixes
 - Use readr and stop relying on system commands (grep, sed, gunzip) to read seqz files
 - Use the package pbapply for progress bar
 - Normalize each sample separately
 - Provide coverage profile of the 2 samples separately, before and after normalization
 - Provide CG-content vs depth profile for each samples, before and after normalization
 - Draw standard "mirrored" BAF (from 0 to 1) in the raw genome view

Also sequenza-utils 3.0.0 is on pypi, it is compatible with python 2.7/3. It adds support from VCF to seqz files and varius cleanup and bug fixes.

All in all the 3.0.0 realease works much better then the legacy version. I strongly encourage to upgrade :-).

I hope you'll enjoy the new release.

Best

Francesco

messages.body_plain:

Em sexta-feira, 8 de março de 2019 16:56:32 UTC-3, emreko...@googlemail.com escreveu:
> Hi Tommy and Francesco,
>
> I am currently struggling with the same question. How to pick the best result for ploidy (and therefore cellularity) when there are several options. It seems that SLPP is not helpful for every case and manual curation of each model fit cannot be the solution (working with n>600 samples).
> @Tommy Did you find a convenient solution in the meantime?
>
> Best
> Emre
>
> On Friday, February 3, 2017 at 12:25:53 PM UTC-5, Tommy Tang wrote:
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-3in_Io0-HWk/WJS8pbwNBeI/AAAAAAAABXE/kEp3fzir7t4xAkJZBMnSa-cjRQzm0b7pwCLcB/s1600/model_filt.jpg>
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-_EOlXrt2XiI/WJS8lp2vUDI/AAAAAAAABXA/LArBQLj9140uCLl8yy_Y-_xO1oxhDDUjQCLcB/s1600/genome_view-2.jpg>
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-xCgmBOKr5Q4/WJS8iEOUyWI/AAAAAAAABW8/vXsDJCo4E9UtPecit2Is_9lgxSNbWwjAwCLcB/s1600/genome_view-1.jpg>
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-wdLHAnTHdXU/WJS8dHMC0cI/AAAAAAAABW4/Fh1T6c9T1Oc2Q63pgte-leqm3W2TMNqGQCLcB/s1600/genome_view-0.jpg>
> >
> > Thanks.
> > Just to make sure, the depth.ratio is the reading depth from the tumors cells of the tumor sample divided by the reading depth of the normal control?
> > Does this depth.ratio takes into account of the tumor purity?
> >
> > simply case:
> >
> > suppose the tumor purity is 0.5, we have 1 normal cell (diploid) and 1 tumor cell (ploidy of 4) sequenced in the tumor sample.
> > we also have 1 normal cell sequenced in the normal control sample.
> >
> > The depth.raio = (2 allele + 4 allele )/2 allele = 3?
> >
> > The genome view of my real sample that has a predicted ploid of 4.6:
> >
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-wdLHAnTHdXU/WJS8dHMC0cI/AAAAAAAABW4/Fh1T6c9T1Oc2Q63pgte-leqm3W2TMNqGQCLcB/s1600/genome_view-0.jpg>
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-xCgmBOKr5Q4/WJS8iEOUyWI/AAAAAAAABW8/vXsDJCo4E9UtPecit2Is_9lgxSNbWwjAwCLcB/s1600/genome_view-1.jpg>
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-_EOlXrt2XiI/WJS8lp2vUDI/AAAAAAAABXA/LArBQLj9140uCLl8yy_Y-_xO1oxhDDUjQCLcB/s1600/genome_view-2.jpg>
> >
> >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-3in_Io0-HWk/WJS8pbwNBeI/AAAAAAAABXE/kEp3fzir7t4xAkJZBMnSa-cjRQzm0b7pwCLcB/s1600/model_filt.jpg>
> > How to read the figures and figure out if the ploidy estimation is correct?
> >
> > The alternative solutions are:
> >
> >
> > "cellularity" "ploidy" "SLPP"
> >
> > 0.69 4.6 0.127104505129711
> >
> > 0.65 5.7 0.116550925080056
> >
> > 0.78 3.1 3.16170360778432e-47
> >
> > I appreciate your help every much!
> >
> > Tommy
> >
> > On Thursday, February 2, 2017 at 6:35:54 PM UTC-6, Francesco Favero wrote:
> > > Hi Tommy,
> > >
> > > Your consideration about the ploidy is correct, the ploidy means more DNA, so if you have an admixture of 1 tetraploid tumor cell and 1 normal cell, you would have 6 alleles in total, 4 from the tumor and 2 from the normal (this will correspond approximately to the proportion of the number of reads),  however the cellularity is still 50%.
> > >
> > > N.BAF and N.ratio are the number of observations we used to calculate the Bf and the dept.ratio, respectively.
> > >
> > > In your case, you have a ploidy estimate of 4.6, that means that and dept.ratio = 1 a segment should have copy number 4.6, however the model consider only integer copy numbers, and a floating copy number would imply a subclonal fraction (and we would treat those scenario as a separate workflow).
> > > So your segment with ratio 0.9 is rightfully correlated with a CNt of 4. The Bf value, quite low, means that the A and B allele are not in even proportion, the model estimates 1 copy of B and 3 copies of A.
> > >
> > > To detect copy gain/los, everything that is estimated bigger then 5 is copy gain, less the 5 is a loss.
> > >
> > > In order to visually inspect the results, you should use the model fit plot, the CP contour plot (cellularity vs ploidy estimates), and visually inspect the chromosome view, to see if the profile looks regular, or there are clear bias in the data.
> > >
> > > The most relevant, in my opinion, is the mode fit with the alternative solution (the pdf with yellow/red halo, and blacks dots all). The black dots are your segments, the colored spots are the position predicted by the model. the importance of the visual inspection is because the human brain can pick up in an instant (with a bit of experience) odds situations, for instance, if aneuploidy is caused by overfitting noise, or if one of the alternative solution make more sense than the top ranked.
> > >
> > > I hope this will help you going on with your results
> > >
> > > Best
> > >
> > > Francesco
> > >

Hi,

Thanks

Em sexta-feira, 26 de janeiro de 2018 20:54:07 UTC-2, jane cao escreveu:
> Hi,
>
> I used sequenza to estimate tumor cellularity and sequenza performed well.   As the mutations file from sequence is in txt format but not vcf format I needed for other analysis, I run VarScan2.4.2 to obtain vcf output.  After comparing the mutation result from sequenza and somatic result from varscan, I noticed that the results from those two programs are not identical.  For example, with the same normal and tumor bam files, sequenza mutations file reported 356 mutations and varscan identified 2017 somatic mutations.  I expected that sequenza and varscan should give identical mutation identifications if the parameter setting are the same, but I couldn't find the information about how sequenza called varscan and how parameters were set up in sequenza R.  Can you let me know what parameter setting I should use to run varscan, so the results from two programs can be identical or at least similar?  The workflows I used for varcan and sequenza are:
>
> VarScan:
>
> samtools mpileup -B -f hg38.fa -q 15 normal.bam tumor.bam | java -Xmx16g -jar VarScan.v2.4.2.jar somatic --min-coverage-normal 10 --min-coverage-tumor 10 --min-var-freq 0.1 --strand-filter 0 --output-vcf
>
> Sequenza:
>
> 1. run "sequenza-utils bam2seq -n normal.bam -t tumor.bam -gc hg38.gc50base.wig.gz -F hg38.fa
> 2. run "sequenza-utils seqz_binning -w 50 -s output_from_1
> 3. run sequenza in R
> input.extrac<-sequenza.extract(inputFile)
> input.extract.CP<-sequenza.fit(input.extract)
> sequenza.results(sequenza.extract=input.extract, cp.table=input.extract.CP)
>
> Thank you for your help!
>
> Jane
>
>
